name: JLR Ingenium PT204
fullName: Jaguar Land Rover Ingenium 2.0L turbocharged DOHC 16-valve inline four (PT204 / AJ200P), 237 hp
summary: JLR's in-house 2.0L turbo petrol four, with both timing chains at the transmission end, timed at 50 degrees after TDC with dedicated locking tools. The intake valves are worked by an electrohydraulic CVVL unit rather than directly by the cam, and both camshafts have VCT phasers. The engine also has 200 bar direct injection, a twin-scroll turbo on a head-integrated manifold, gear-driven twin balancers, and an aluminum block with cast-iron liners. Rebuild order is driven by the rear chain drive and by the CVVL unit, which needs clean oil, a reset of its brake units and a software calibration.

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 237 hp, 251 lb-ft (240 PS / 340 N·m) in the 2018 US Discovery Sport

facts.label: Block material
facts.value: Deep-skirt aluminum with thin-wall interference-fit cast-iron liners

facts.label: Timing drive
facts.value: Two chains (crank to idler, idler to cams) at the transmission end; timed at 50 degrees ATDC with locking tools

facts.label: Valvetrain
facts.value: Electrohydraulic CVVL on the intake (cam drives oil pumps, not valves); roller followers on the exhaust; VCT on both cams

facts.label: Fuel injection
facts.value: 200 bar central direct injection; HP fuel pump driven by an exhaust-cam lobe

facts.label: Turbocharger
facts.value: Twin-scroll, on an exhaust manifold cast into the head

facts.label: Balancers
facts.value: Two counter-rotating shafts at twice crank speed, gear-driven

facts.label: Oil capacity
facts.value: About 7.0 L (7.4 qt) of 0W-20 meeting STJLR.51.5122

notes: The timing chains are at the rear (transmission) end. Any chain work means removing the transmission and drive plate, so most shops pull the whole engine.

The engine is timed at 50 degrees after TDC, not at TDC. Turn it clockwise only, and set it with JLR-303-1630 (crank pulley lock), JLR-303-1635 (camshaft setting tool) and JLR-303-1636 (VCT lock). Turn the crank with JLR-303-1656 (crank rotation tool).

Other JLR tools used here: JLR-303-1653 (head bolts), JLR-303-1639 and JLR-303-1647 (CVVL), JLR-303-1712 and JLR-303-1674A (rear seal), JLR-303-1628 (front seal), 303-1433 (front cover alignment), JLR-310-254/255/256/257 and 310-198 (injectors), 205-053 (oil pump sprocket), 303-252 (valve springs).

Single-use parts: head bolts, drive plate bolts, crank pulley bolts, VCT center bolts, all timing guides and both tensioners, turbo nuts and banjo bolts, injector seals and clamps, and every gasket and O-ring. HP fuel lines have a limited number of tightening cycles.

The CVVL unit cannot be serviced and must never be turned upside down. After it has been off, reset its brake units, run the JLR software calibration and build oil pressure by cranking before the first start.

Known failure modes: VCT actuator internal seal leaks causing rattle and cam timing codes (2018 bulletin); timing chain and tensioner wear; oil degradation and sludge in the CVVL and high-pressure oil galleries in short-trip urban use; CVVL-related misfires; coolant leaks at the thermostat housing.

Spec gaps: no verified values were found for main cap bolts, rod bolts, idler sprocket bolt, ring gaps, bearing clearances or head flatness. Take them from JLR TOPIx, the factory service information system. Many specs here come from the JLR manual for the 2020-on Defender, which uses the same Ingenium I4 2.0L petrol; confirm against the 2018 Discovery Sport manual.
Usually sent out: valve seat work and any liner or block repair. JLR offers only one piston size and no serviceable valve guides, so a badly worn bore or guide usually means a new block or head.

phases.name: Preparation and removal
phases.summary: Diagnose, gather the JLR tools and renew-only parts, then get the engine out and onto a stand.

phases.name: External teardown
phases.summary: Strip the accessories, turbo, intake, direct-injection fuel system and sensors down to the bare long block.

phases.name: Timing drive at the rear
phases.summary: Lock the engine at 50 degrees after TDC, then remove both chains, the phasers, the drive plate and the end covers.

phases.name: Cylinder head and valvetrain
phases.summary: Lift off the CVVL unit and camshaft carrier, then the head, and strip the valves.

phases.name: Short-block teardown
phases.summary: Remove the oil pan, oil pump, windage tray, pistons, crankshaft and balancer shafts.

phases.name: Cleaning and measurement
phases.summary: Clean every gallery, read the factory grade codes and measure what decides reuse.

phases.name: Machine-shop decisions
phases.summary: Decide what can be machined, what must be replaced, and which bearing grades to fit.

phases.name: Short-block assembly
phases.summary: Fit the balancers, crankshaft, pistons, oil pump, oil pan and front cover, in that order.

phases.name: Head and camshaft carrier
phases.summary: Build and torque the head, then fit the followers, camshafts and camshaft carrier.

phases.name: Timing with locking tools
phases.summary: Lock the crank and cams, fit both chains with new guides and tensioners, then close up the rear of the engine.

phases.name: External reassembly
phases.summary: Refit the CVVL unit, direct-injection fuel system, intake, oil cooler, turbo (with a primed oil feed) and accessories.

phases.name: Installation and first start
phases.summary: Refill, calibrate the CVVL unit, build oil pressure without firing, then start and check.

steps.title: Read codes before removal
steps.action: With the engine still in the vehicle, scan the engine computer (PCM) and save every stored code and the camshaft timing data. VCT codes (P052A, P0011, P000A) point at the phasers and chain; repeated misfire codes (P0300, P0316, P1315) point at the CVVL unit.
steps.why: Once the engine is apart you can no longer tell a phaser fault from a stretched chain or a sticking CVVL solenoid.
tools: JLR-approved diagnostic tool or capable scan tool

mistakes.title: Clearing codes before recording them
mistakes.what: Clearing the codes or disconnecting the battery before the stored codes and cam timing data are saved.
mistakes.consequence: The evidence separating a leaking VCT actuator, a worn chain and a failing CVVL unit is lost, so the wrong part may be reused.
mistakes.prevent: Save a full scan report, including the VCT and misfire codes and their freeze frames, before anything is unplugged.

mistakes.title: Blaming the chain for VCT codes
mistakes.what: Blaming VCT codes on chain stretch, renewing the chain and refitting the old intake VCT actuator.
mistakes.consequence: JLR traced these codes and the rattle on 2018 engines to an internal seal in the VCT actuator, so the fault comes back.
mistakes.prevent: Treat VCT codes as a possible phaser fault, and budget a new intake VCT actuator on a 2018 engine that has them.
mistakes.detect: Rattle from the rear of the engine with VCT codes stored on the scan report.

mistakes.title: Ignoring a history of CVVL misfires
mistakes.what: Writing off repeated P0300, P0316 or P1315 codes as plugs or coils and refitting the original CVVL unit.
mistakes.consequence: The misfire returns after the rebuild and the CVVL unit has to come off again to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: If those codes are in the history, follow JLR's diagnosis and plan for a new CVVL unit before reassembly.

steps.title: Sample the old oil
steps.action: Drain a clean sample of the used oil into a bottle and note its smell, color and any sludge before draining the rest.
steps.why: JLR asks for an oil sample with any returned CVVL unit because degraded oil and sludge are the known killers of this engine's high-pressure oil circuits.

mistakes.title: Skipping the used oil sample
mistakes.what: Draining all the old oil straight into the waste drum without keeping a sample.
mistakes.consequence: You lose the evidence of sludge or degraded oil that explains a CVVL or VCT failure, and JLR asks for an oil sample with a returned CVVL unit.
mistakes.prevent: Catch about 100 ml in a clean, labeled bottle before the rest drains.

mistakes.title: Shrugging off sludge or milky oil
mistakes.what: Noticing sludge, a burnt smell or a milky emulsion in the old oil but not chasing its cause.
mistakes.consequence: Sludge goes on to block the new CVVL unit and high-pressure galleries, and coolant in the oil corrodes the new bearings.
mistakes.prevent: Act on what you saw: sludge means a full gallery clean and a hard look at the CVVL unit; coolant means pressure tests.

steps.title: Run a compression test
steps.action: With the spark plugs out and fuel injection disabled, check compression on all four cylinders and record the numbers.
steps.why: A timing-tool maker recommends a compression check before the head comes off on this interference engine; it tells you whether valves were already hit.

mistakes.title: Skipping the compression check
mistakes.what: Taking the head off without compression numbers for each cylinder.
mistakes.consequence: On an interference engine you can no longer tell whether a valve was bent by a jumped chain, and a bent valve can be refitted unnoticed.
mistakes.prevent: Test and record all four cylinders before teardown, and follow up a low cylinder with a leak-down test.
mistakes.detect: One cylinder reads clearly lower than the others.

mistakes.title: Cranking with fuel injection live
mistakes.what: Running the compression test with the injectors still connected.
mistakes.consequence: Fuel is sprayed into the cylinders, washing the bores and diluting the oil, and the readings are not trustworthy.
mistakes.prevent: Disable fuel injection and remove all the plugs before cranking.

steps.title: Order renew-only parts
steps.action: Before teardown, order the parts JLR treats as single use: head bolts, drive plate bolts, crank pulley bolts, VCT actuator bolts, all timing guides and both tensioners, turbo nuts and banjo bolts, injector seals and every gasket and O-ring.
steps.why: The procedures mark these parts 'renew' every time they are disturbed, so the rebuild stalls without them.

mistakes.title: Reusing single-use bolts to keep going
mistakes.what: Refitting old head, drive plate, VCT or pulley bolts to keep going when a part is missing mid-build.
mistakes.consequence: Single-use bolts that have already been torqued no longer give the designed clamp, so the head gasket, drive plate or a phaser can slip.
mistakes.prevent: Order the full renew list before teardown and put every removed single-use bolt in a scrap tray as it comes out.

mistakes.title: Ordering parts without the VIN
mistakes.what: Ordering parts by model and year alone instead of from the VIN.
mistakes.consequence: Superseded parts such as the revised VCT actuator and VCT solenoids can be missed, so an old-spec part goes back in and the bulletin fault returns.
mistakes.prevent: Order by VIN in the parts catalog and check for any open bulletins or service actions on the engine.

mistakes.title: Leaving injector and CVVL parts off the order
mistakes.what: Leaving the injector refit kit, injector clamps and CVVL gasket off the parts order.
mistakes.consequence: The build stalls at the injectors, or old seals are reused and leak fuel or combustion gas.
mistakes.prevent: Add a complete injector refit kit and the CVVL and camshaft carrier gaskets to the order up front.

steps.title: Gather the JLR timing tools
steps.action: Collect the crankshaft pulley locking tool JLR-303-1630, camshaft setting tool JLR-303-1635, VCT actuator locking tool JLR-303-1636 and crank rotation tool JLR-303-1656, plus the CVVL and seal tools listed in later steps.
steps.why: This engine has no simple timing pins; correct cam-to-crank timing is only achievable with the setting and locking tools.

mistakes.title: Timing by eye without the tools
mistakes.what: Timing the chains by lining up marks by eye, without the crank lock, camshaft setting tool or VCT lock.
mistakes.consequence: A cam can end up a tooth out or a phaser twisted on its bolt, giving cam timing codes, poor running or valve-to-piston contact.
mistakes.prevent: Have JLR-303-1630, JLR-303-1635 and JLR-303-1636, or an equivalent kit, on the bench before the covers come off.

mistakes.title: Buying the diesel Ingenium timing kit
mistakes.what: Buying a timing kit for the Ingenium diesel because the name matches.
mistakes.consequence: The tools do not fit the petrol engine, and forcing them can mark the camshafts or set the timing wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Check that the kit lists the AJ200P/PT204 petrol engine codes before the job starts.

steps.title: Remove the engine assembly
steps.action: Following the vehicle procedure, separate the transmission and lift the engine out with the JLR lifting kit, an engine crane and a helper.
steps.why: The timing chains sit at the transmission end, so the transmission and drive plate must come off before any chain work is possible.

mistakes.title: Lifting on improvised points
mistakes.what: Slinging the engine from brackets, the intake or pipework instead of from the JLR lifting kit points.
mistakes.consequence: Brackets bend or plastic parts break, and the engine can tip and strike the body or fall.
mistakes.prevent: Use the JLR engine lifting kit and a helper to guide the engine out.

mistakes.title: Lifting with a connection still attached
mistakes.what: Starting to lift with the crane while a harness ground, hose or connector is still attached.
mistakes.consequence: The harness or a hose is torn, adding damaged parts to the job.
mistakes.prevent: Walk around the engine and check that every harness, ground and hose is free before taking the weight.

steps.title: Mount the engine on a stand
steps.action: Bolt the engine to a stand using the JLR engine stand adapter so it can be rotated for top and bottom access.

mistakes.title: Skipping the engine stand adapter
mistakes.what: Bolting on a generic stand plate without the JLR stand adapter.
mistakes.consequence: Bolts may have too little thread engagement in the aluminum block, and the engine can shift or fall when rotated.
mistakes.prevent: Use the JLR stand adapter and make sure every bolt has full thread engagement before rotating the engine.

steps.title: Drain oil and coolant
steps.action: Pull the side-mounted oil pan drain plug and drain the oil, then drain any coolant left in the block and pipes. Refit the plug with a new washer.

spec.note: oil pan drain plug, new washer

mistakes.title: Stripping the drain plug thread
mistakes.what: Refitting the drain plug on the old washer and tightening it hard to stop a weep.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminum pan thread strips, which means a thread repair or a new pan.
mistakes.prevent: Fit a new washer and torque the plug to spec.

steps.title: Strip NVH pads and covers
steps.action: Unclip and remove the foam and laminate NVH (noise, vibration and harshness) pads from the block sides, head and timing cover area.

steps.title: Remove coolant pipes and degas bottle
steps.action: Unbolt the coolant pipes and hoses around the engine and remove the coolant degas separator, checking each O-ring as it comes out.

mistakes.title: Reusing flattened coolant pipe O-rings
mistakes.what: Refitting the O-rings from the coolant pipes and degas separator without inspecting them.
mistakes.consequence: Coolant weeps from the joints once the engine is hot and pressurized.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect each O-ring as it comes out and replace any that are flattened, cut or hard.

steps.title: Remove breather and purge valve
steps.action: Disconnect the breather pipe connectors and remove the breather pipe, then unbolt the evaporative purge valve assembly.

mistakes.title: Forcing brittle breather connectors
mistakes.what: Levering or twisting quick-release breather connectors off without releasing their catches.
mistakes.consequence: Broken connectors leak crankcase gases or let in unmetered air, setting fuel trim codes.
mistakes.prevent: Release each catch fully and replace any connector that cracks.

steps.title: Pull the oil dipstick tube
steps.action: Remove the bolt and lift out the oil dipstick tube, discarding its O-ring.

mistakes.title: Reusing the dipstick tube O-ring
mistakes.what: Putting the old dipstick tube O-ring back in.
mistakes.consequence: The tube weeps oil and can let unmetered air into the crankcase.
mistakes.prevent: Fit a new O-ring to the tube on reassembly.

steps.title: Remove belt and idler pulleys
steps.action: Release the accessory belt tension, remove the belt, then remove the two idler pulley covers and pulleys, noting where each pulley came from.
steps.why: The two idlers use different bolt sizes and must go back in their original positions.

mistakes.title: Not marking the idler positions
mistakes.what: Removing the two idler pulleys together without noting which came from where.
mistakes.consequence: Later you have two similar pulleys and no record, so a guess decides which goes where.
mistakes.prevent: Bag and label each idler with its bolt as it comes off.

steps.title: Remove the generator
steps.action: Disconnect the battery cable and connector, remove the two bolts and lift off the generator.

steps.title: Lift off the engine harness
steps.action: Unplug every sensor, actuator and injector connector, release the harness clips and brackets, and lift the engine harness off as one piece.
steps.why: Labeling the connectors now saves guesswork later; the harness has dozens of plugs, including four CVVL solenoids.

mistakes.title: Unplugging without labels
mistakes.what: Lifting the harness off without labeling or photographing the connectors.
mistakes.consequence: Connectors are swapped or missed on reassembly, giving codes, misfires or a no-start.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph the harness in place and tag every connector before releasing it.

mistakes.title: Breaking a CVVL solenoid connector
mistakes.what: Prying the CVVL solenoid connectors off, or moving the CVVL unit with the harness still attached.
mistakes.consequence: JLR notes these connectors are very easily damaged, and the CVVL unit is not serviceable, so a broken connector can mean a new unit.
mistakes.prevent: Release each latch by hand and move the harness clear before the CVVL unit is touched.

steps.title: Remove the coolant pump
steps.action: Hold the pulley, remove its three bolts, then remove the six pump bolts and the coolant pump.
steps.mistake: Reusing a pump whose gasket is damaged; the gasket is not sold separately, so a damaged one means a new pump.

mistakes.title: Prying the coolant pump off
mistakes.what: Driving a screwdriver into the pump joint to break it free.
mistakes.consequence: The pump gasket is not sold separately, so a damaged gasket means a new pump.
mistakes.prevent: Remove all six bolts and free the pump gently, without wedging anything into the joint.

mistakes.title: Not holding the pump pulley
mistakes.what: Loosening the pulley bolts without holding the pulley.
mistakes.consequence: The pulley turns with the wrench and the bolt heads round off before they break loose.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the pulley with a suitable holding tool while loosening its bolts.

steps.title: Remove turbo oil feed pipe
steps.action: Unbolt the support bracket, then remove the turbo oil feed pipe, cutting off the trapped lower sealing washers and discarding both banjo bolts and all four washers.
steps.why: Banjo bolts and washers on the oil feed are single use; a reused washer is a common source of oil leaks onto a hot turbo.

mistakes.title: Leaving turbo oil ports open
mistakes.what: Disconnecting the turbo oil feed and leaving the turbo and block ports uncovered.
mistakes.consequence: Dirt falls into the bearing housing or feed and is carried into the bearings on first start, a classic cause of turbo failure.
mistakes.prevent: Cap or tape every oil port as soon as the pipe comes off.

mistakes.title: Kinking the oil feed pipe
mistakes.what: Bending the feed pipe to get it out past the bracket.
mistakes.consequence: A pipe that is crushed or collapsed inside restricts oil to the turbo and starves its bearings.
mistakes.prevent: Remove the bracket first and inspect the pipe; fit a new one if it is kinked or damaged.

steps.title: Remove turbo heat shields
steps.action: Remove the bolts and lift off the turbo heat shields, discarding the one bolt the procedure lists as renew-only.

mistakes.title: Reusing the renew-only shield bolt
mistakes.what: Reusing the heat shield bolt the procedure lists as renew-only.
mistakes.consequence: The bolt can loosen with heat cycles and let the shield rattle or shift.
mistakes.prevent: Put the renew-only bolt in the scrap tray and fit a new one at reassembly.

steps.title: Remove turbo oil return
steps.action: Remove the bolt and pull the turbo oil return pipe, discarding its two O-rings.

mistakes.title: Leaving the oil return port open
mistakes.what: Leaving the turbo oil return opening in the block uncovered.
mistakes.consequence: Debris can drop straight into the oil pan and reach the oil pickup.
mistakes.prevent: Push a clean plug or taped cap into the return port before moving on.

steps.title: Lift off the turbocharger
steps.action: Remove and discard the four nuts holding the turbo to the head's integrated exhaust manifold, lift the turbo off and discard the gasket.
steps.why: The exhaust manifold is cast into the head, so the turbo bolts straight to the head and must come off before the head can.

mistakes.title: Dropping debris into the exhaust ports
mistakes.what: Letting gasket crumbs, a nut or rust flakes fall into the exhaust passages of the head's integrated manifold.
mistakes.consequence: Loose debris is blown into the turbine on first start and wrecks it with foreign-object damage.
mistakes.prevent: Cover the manifold outlet as soon as the turbo is off and check it is clear before refitting.

mistakes.title: Forcing seized turbo studs
mistakes.what: Forcing corroded turbo nuts off without penetrating oil or heat.
mistakes.consequence: A stud snaps off in the cylinder head itself, since the manifold is cast into the head, so the head needs stud extraction or machining.
mistakes.prevent: Soak the nuts, work them back and forth, and stop if a stud starts to twist.

steps.title: Remove the oil cooler
steps.action: Disconnect the coolant hose, remove the seven bolts and remove the oil cooler from the side of the block below the turbo, discarding its metal gasket.
steps.why: The cooler sits under the turbo, so the turbo has to come off first.

mistakes.title: Letting coolant into oil ports
mistakes.what: Removing the oil cooler while coolant is still in the block, so it runs into the open oil passages.
mistakes.consequence: Coolant left in the oil circuit corrodes bearings and mixes with fresh oil on first start.
mistakes.prevent: Drain the coolant first and blow out any coolant that reaches the oil ports.

steps.title: Remove the intake manifold
steps.action: Loosen the captive bolts, lift off the plastic intake manifold with its throttle and manifold pressure (MAP) sensor, and discard the four port seals.

mistakes.title: Leaving intake ports uncovered
mistakes.what: Leaving the intake ports open after the manifold comes off.
mistakes.consequence: Bolts or debris dropped into a port end up in a cylinder or caught behind a valve.
mistakes.prevent: Tape over every intake port as soon as the manifold is off.

steps.title: Remove the thermostat housing
steps.action: Remove the four bolts and the thermostat housing, keeping the gasket only if it is undamaged.
steps.mistake: Ignoring seepage at the thermostat housing; JLR has bulletins on coolant leaks from this housing's welded spigot and gasket.

mistakes.title: Ignoring a weeping thermostat housing
mistakes.what: Wiping dried coolant off the thermostat housing spigot or gasket and refitting the housing as it was.
mistakes.consequence: The thermostat housing is a known coolant leak point on the Ingenium petrol, so the leak returns and the engine can run low on coolant.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the housing and spigot for cracks or seepage marks and replace the housing or gasket at any sign of a leak.
mistakes.detect: Crusty coolant residue on the housing or on the block below it.

mistakes.title: Reusing a marginal housing gasket
mistakes.what: Reusing a thermostat housing gasket with a crease or compression set because it looks intact.
mistakes.consequence: The housing seeps coolant after a few heat cycles.
mistakes.prevent: Reuse the gasket only if it is truly undamaged; otherwise fit a new one.

steps.title: Remove HP fuel lines
steps.action: Unbolt and remove both high-pressure fuel lines, and count the paint marks on each before deciding whether it can go back on.
steps.why: JLR allows each HP line a limited number of tightening cycles and has you paint-mark it after each one.

spec.note: maximum tightening cycles per HP line; paint-mark after each

steps.mistake: Reusing an HP line that has already been tightened its maximum number of times, which risks a fuel leak at 200 bar.

mistakes.title: Refitting an HP line at its limit
mistakes.what: Tightening an HP fuel line again when it already carries its maximum number of paint marks.
mistakes.consequence: The union may no longer seal at direct-injection pressure, and fuel leaking beside a hot engine is a fire risk.
mistakes.prevent: Count the paint marks on each line and replace any line that has used up its permitted tightening cycles.

mistakes.title: Leaving the high-pressure ports open
mistakes.what: Leaving the HP fuel line ports on the pump and rail uncapped on the bench.
mistakes.consequence: Grit gets into the pump outlet and rail while the engine is apart and is flushed into the injectors on first start.
mistakes.prevent: Cap every fuel opening with clean plugs and work with lint-free cloths.

mistakes.title: Losing count of line tightening cycles
mistakes.what: Cleaning off or not counting the paint marks on the HP lines before refitting.
mistakes.consequence: A line past its permitted tightening cycles goes back on and can leak fuel at high pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Count the marks on removal, tag the lines, and scrap any that are at the limit.

steps.title: Remove the HP fuel pump
steps.action: Back the two pump bolts out one turn at a time, alternating, until the spring pressure from the cam lobe is gone, then lift the pump off.
steps.why: The pump plunger is preloaded by a lobe on the exhaust camshaft; uneven release can crack the flange or cock the pump.
steps.mistake: Unscrewing one bolt fully while the other still holds spring load.

mistakes.title: Unbolting the HP fuel pump one side first
mistakes.what: Unscrewing one pump bolt fully while the other still holds the cam lobe spring load.
mistakes.consequence: The pump tilts under spring pressure, which can crack its flange or damage the tappet and its bore.
mistakes.prevent: Back both bolts out one turn at a time, alternating, until the spring load has gone.

mistakes.title: Leaving pump ports uncapped
mistakes.what: Setting the removed HP fuel pump down with its inlet and outlet open.
mistakes.consequence: Dirt enters the pump and is pushed into the injectors when the engine runs.
mistakes.prevent: Cap the pump ports and store the pump in a clean bag.

steps.title: Remove the HP fuel pump tappet
steps.action: Lift the HP fuel pump tappet out of its bore in the camshaft carrier and keep it clean.

mistakes.title: Losing track of the pump tappet
mistakes.what: Leaving the HP fuel pump tappet loose on the bench or letting it fall into the camshaft carrier.
mistakes.consequence: A lost or damaged tappet means waiting for a part, and a scuffed one wears the pump lobe on the camshaft.
mistakes.prevent: Bag the tappet, inspect its contact face, and check the pump lobe when you inspect the camshafts.

steps.title: Remove coils and spark plugs
steps.action: Remove the four coil bolts and coils, then remove the spark plugs.
steps.why: With the plugs out, the engine turns without compression fighting the timing tools later.

mistakes.title: Not cleaning the plug wells first
mistakes.what: Removing the plugs without blowing out the wells.
mistakes.consequence: Grit falls into the cylinders and the plug threads, scoring bores and spoiling plug seating later.
mistakes.prevent: Blow the wells clean before loosening the plugs; the plug seats must be clean to seal later.

steps.title: Remove the fuel rail
steps.action: Remove the four rail bolts and lift the fuel rail away from the injectors.

mistakes.title: Leaving rail openings uncovered
mistakes.what: Setting the rail aside with its injector cups and line ports open.
mistakes.consequence: Debris in the rail is flushed into the new injectors on first start.
mistakes.prevent: Cap all rail openings and keep the rail in a clean bag.

steps.title: Extract the fuel injectors
steps.action: Discard the injector spring clamps, fit the JLR injector remover with a slide hammer, and pull each centrally mounted injector straight out of the head.
steps.why: Combustion deposits grip the injector tips; the puller keeps the pull straight so the bore and nozzle are not damaged. The CVVL unit cannot come off until the injectors are out.
steps.mistake: Prying injectors out sideways, which can damage the injector or its bore in the head.

mistakes.title: Levering injectors out sideways
mistakes.what: Prying a stuck injector out with a pry bar instead of the JLR remover and slide hammer.
mistakes.consequence: The injector body or its bore in the head is damaged, and a marked bore will not hold a new seal.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the JLR injector remover and pull each injector straight out along its own axis.

mistakes.title: Lifting the CVVL before the injectors
mistakes.what: Unbolting and lifting the CVVL unit while the injectors are still in the head.
mistakes.consequence: JLR has the injectors removed first; lifting the CVVL unit around them risks damaging the injectors or the unit itself.
mistakes.prevent: Remove all four injectors before the CVVL bolts are touched.

mistakes.title: Knocking the injector nozzle tip
mistakes.what: Gripping, tapping or setting down an injector on its tip.
mistakes.consequence: A damaged tip changes the spray pattern, causing misfire and deposits, and means a new injector.
mistakes.prevent: Handle injectors by their bodies, protect the tips, and keep them in a clean tray.

steps.title: Discard all injector seals
steps.action: Cut off and discard each injector's Teflon combustion seal, O-ring and washer.
steps.why: These seals are single use and are sized on the injector at refit with special tools.

mistakes.title: Reusing a heat-cycled Teflon seal
mistakes.what: Leaving an injector's original Teflon combustion seal on because it looks fine.
mistakes.consequence: A Teflon seal that has been heated in service cannot reseal, so combustion gas leaks past the injector.
mistakes.prevent: Cut off and discard every Teflon seal, O-ring and washer.
mistakes.detect: Ticking or a combustion leak at the injector after start-up.

mistakes.title: Scoring the injector seal groove
mistakes.what: Cutting the old Teflon seal off with a knife or pick that marks the groove.
mistakes.consequence: A scratched groove leaks past the new seal and the injector may need replacing.
mistakes.prevent: Use the proper seal cutting tool and avoid touching the tip.

steps.title: Remove cam sensors and solenoids
steps.action: Remove both camshaft position sensors, then the four bolts holding the two VCT solenoids, and pull the solenoids out of the upper timing cover.
steps.why: The VCT solenoids reach through the upper timing cover to the phaser center bolts, so they must come out before the cover will lift off.

mistakes.title: Lifting the cover with solenoids in
mistakes.what: Prying off the upper timing cover with the VCT solenoids still fitted through it.
mistakes.consequence: The solenoids are bent against the phaser bolts or the cover cracks.
mistakes.prevent: Remove both VCT solenoids before any cover bolts.

mistakes.title: Leaving the solenoid bores open
mistakes.what: Leaving the VCT solenoid bores uncovered with the cover off.
mistakes.consequence: Dirt enters the phaser oil feed and can make a phaser stick, giving cam timing codes.
mistakes.prevent: Cover the bores and keep the solenoids in a clean bag.

steps.title: Remove the knock sensors
steps.action: Note the exact position of each knock sensor, then remove both.
steps.why: Knock sensor orientation affects signal quality; the procedure has you refit them where they came from.

mistakes.title: Not recording knock sensor positions
mistakes.what: Removing both knock sensors without marking their positions and orientation.
mistakes.consequence: Refitted in the wrong place, they read knock poorly, so the PCM retards timing or misses real knock.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph and mark each sensor's position before removal.

steps.title: Remove block-mounted sensors
steps.action: Remove the piston cooling jet solenoid, the vacuum pipe connector and the crankshaft position sensor, keeping their O-rings for inspection.

steps.title: Remove filter housing and filler
steps.action: Remove the oil filler pipe, unscrew the filter cap and discard the element, then remove the three housing bolts and the oil filter housing, discarding its five O-rings.

steps.title: Remove the vent oil separator
steps.action: Loosen the captive bolts and lift off the engine vent oil separator, discarding its gasket.

steps.title: Remove the upper timing cover
steps.action: Remove the NVH pad, the twelve bolts and the upper timing cover at the transmission end of the head, and discard its gasket.
steps.why: On this engine both chains are at the rear, so everything timing-related starts here rather than at the pulley end.

mistakes.title: Prying the cover by its sealing face
mistakes.what: Driving a screwdriver into the cover joint to free the upper timing cover.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminum sealing face is gouged and the cover leaks oil after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Break the seal gently at a robust point and never lever on the sealing faces.

steps.title: Rotate to the timing position
steps.action: Fit the crank rotation tool and turn the crankshaft clockwise only until the pulley mark points down and both cam marks point up. That is 50 degrees after TDC on cylinder 1.
steps.why: JLR sets this engine's timing at 50 degrees after TDC rather than at TDC, so no piston is at the top while the cams are locked.

spec.note: after TDC, cylinder 1; pulley mark at 6 o'clock, cam marks at 12 o'clock

steps.mistake: Looking for TDC marks, or turning the engine counter-clockwise to reach the marks.

mistakes.title: Hunting for TDC marks
mistakes.what: Looking for a TDC mark, or turning the engine counter-clockwise to reach the timing marks.
mistakes.consequence: The engine is locked in the wrong position, or reverse rotation lets the chain go slack and jump a tooth.
mistakes.prevent: Remember the lock position is 50 degrees after TDC and only ever turn the crank clockwise.

mistakes.title: Turning the engine on a cam sprocket
mistakes.what: Turning the engine with a wrench on a phaser bolt or cam sprocket instead of at the crank.
mistakes.consequence: The load goes through the chain and phasers and can loosen a phaser bolt; the timing tool maker warns against it.
mistakes.prevent: Turn the engine only at the crankshaft with the JLR rotation tool.

mistakes.title: Stopping one revolution out
mistakes.what: Stopping the first time the pulley mark points down, with the cam marks pointing down instead of up.
mistakes.consequence: The cams are 180 degrees out from the locking position, and the setting tool will not fit or is forced on wrongly.
mistakes.prevent: If the cam marks are not at 12 o'clock, turn the crank one more full turn clockwise.

mistakes.title: Forcing past a hard stop
mistakes.what: Pushing harder when the crank meets hard resistance on the way to the marks.
mistakes.consequence: On this interference engine a hard stop can be a valve touching a piston after a chain jumped, and forcing it bends the valve.
mistakes.prevent: If the crank stops solid with the plugs out, stop and find out why before turning further.

steps.title: Fit the camshaft setting tool
steps.action: Bolt the camshaft setting tool across the camshafts and tighten its two bolts.

spec.note: tool bolts

steps.mistake: Forcing the tool on when the cam marks are not aligned, instead of rotating the crank further.

mistakes.title: Forcing the camshaft setting tool on
mistakes.what: Tapping the setting tool into place although the cam marks are not quite at 12 o'clock.
mistakes.consequence: The tool twists a camshaft against the chain, so the engine is locked in a false position and may be timed wrong.
mistakes.prevent: If the tool will not drop on freely, keep turning the crank clockwise until the marks align.

mistakes.title: Overtightening the setting tool bolts
mistakes.what: Cranking the camshaft setting tool bolts tight instead of to their low specified torque.
mistakes.consequence: The tool bolts strip their threads in the aluminum, leaving holes to repair.
mistakes.prevent: Tighten the tool bolts to the specified torque only.

steps.title: Fit the VCT locking tool
steps.action: Bolt the VCT actuator locking tool over both phasers and tighten its two bolts.
steps.why: The tool holds the phaser sprockets still while their center bolts are broken loose, so the chain and cams cannot jump.

spec.note: tool bolts

mistakes.title: Cracking phaser bolts without the VCT lock
mistakes.what: Breaking the phaser center bolts loose with only the camshaft setting tool holding the cams.
mistakes.consequence: The loosening torque goes through the setting tool and camshafts, which can twist the tool or mark the cams.
mistakes.prevent: Fit and torque the VCT locking tool before any phaser bolt is touched.

steps.title: Lock the crankshaft pulley
steps.action: Fit the crankshaft pulley locking tool to the front pulley and lock it in place.

mistakes.title: Leaving the crank unlocked
mistakes.what: Removing the chains without the crank pulley locking tool fitted.
mistakes.consequence: The crank can rotate once the chain is off, losing the timing position and risking piston contact with open valves.
mistakes.prevent: Lock the pulley before the tensioners or chains are removed and leave it until the chains are back on.

steps.title: Break both phaser bolts loose
steps.action: Break both VCT actuator center bolts loose but leave them threaded in.
steps.why: The bolts are tight and need the locking tools to react against; leaving them in keeps the phasers seated until the tensioner is out.
steps.mistake: Removing the center bolts completely at this stage.

mistakes.title: Taking the phaser bolts right out
mistakes.what: Removing the VCT center bolts completely while cracking them loose.
mistakes.consequence: The phasers are no longer held to the cams while the tensioner is still on, so the sprockets can shift off their marks.
mistakes.prevent: Break each bolt loose but leave it threaded in until the tensioner and VCT lock are off, as JLR cautions.

mistakes.title: Removing the tensioner before cracking bolts
mistakes.what: Removing the secondary tensioner before the phaser bolts are broken loose.
mistakes.consequence: With the chain slack the sprockets can shift as the bolts are loosened, and the cams can move off their marks.
mistakes.prevent: Follow the JLR order: lock everything, break both center bolts loose, then remove the tensioner.

steps.title: Remove the secondary tensioner
steps.action: Unscrew and discard the hydraulic upper (secondary) chain tensioner.

steps.title: Remove the VCT locking tool
steps.action: Remove the two bolts and lift off the VCT actuator locking tool so the phasers can come out.

steps.title: Label and remove the phasers
steps.action: Mark each phaser intake or exhaust, then remove and discard the center bolts and lift both VCT actuators off their camshafts.
steps.why: Each VCT actuator is matched to its camshaft, and the two are not interchangeable.
steps.mistake: Swapping the intake and exhaust phasers on reassembly.

mistakes.title: Swapping the intake and exhaust phasers
mistakes.what: Leaving the two VCT actuators unmarked and refitting them on the wrong camshafts.
mistakes.consequence: Each actuator is matched to its own cam, so swapped actuators give the wrong timing range, cam timing codes and poor running.
mistakes.prevent: Mark each phaser intake or exhaust as it comes off and check the part numbers before refitting.

mistakes.title: Refitting the suspect intake VCT actuator
mistakes.what: Refitting the original intake VCT actuator on a 2018 engine with a history of rattle or VCT codes.
mistakes.consequence: The internal seal JLR found to be below specification keeps leaking, so the rattle and codes return.
mistakes.prevent: Replace the intake VCT actuator with the current part when the engine is in the bulletin range or shows the symptoms.

steps.title: Remove the secondary chain guides
steps.action: Remove the bolts and the three secondary (upper) chain guides, and discard them.

mistakes.title: Reusing the old secondary chain guides
mistakes.what: Refitting worn secondary chain guides because they look serviceable.
mistakes.consequence: Worn guides let the chain flap and wear faster, and a broken guide can let the chain jump on an interference engine.
mistakes.prevent: Treat all guides as renew-only and fit the new set.

steps.title: Lift off the secondary chain
steps.action: Lift the secondary chain off the idler sprocket. Before scrapping it, compare its length with a new chain to see how far it has stretched.

mistakes.title: Scrapping the chain unchecked
mistakes.what: Throwing the old secondary chain away without comparing its length to a new one.
mistakes.consequence: You lose the evidence of drive wear that helps explain the fault and judge the phasers and tensioners.
mistakes.prevent: Hang the old and new chains side by side and note the stretch before scrapping the old one.

steps.title: Remove the drive plate
steps.action: With the crank locked at the pulley, remove and discard the eight drive plate bolts and lift off the drive plate with its reluctor ring.
steps.why: The rear crank seal and the lower timing cover sit behind the drive plate.

mistakes.title: Damaging the drive plate reluctor ring
mistakes.what: Levering the drive plate off or setting it down on its reluctor ring.
mistakes.consequence: A bent or nicked ring gives the crankshaft position sensor a bad signal, causing misfire codes or a no-start.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the plate off square and store it flat on a clean surface away from the reluctor teeth.

mistakes.title: Unbolting the drive plate without the crank lock
mistakes.what: Loosening the drive plate bolts with the crank held by a pry bar instead of the pulley locking tool.
mistakes.consequence: The crank rotates off its timing position with the primary chain still on.
mistakes.prevent: Keep the crank pulley lock fitted while the drive plate bolts are broken loose.

steps.title: Extract the rear crank seal
steps.action: Bolt the JLR seal remover to the crank flange on its dowel, drill one hole through the seal at the set depth between 9 and 3 o'clock, then thread in the screw and pull the seal with a slide hammer.
steps.why: The drilling depth is fixed by the tool so the bit cannot reach the crank flange or the cover.
steps.mistake: Drilling without the depth spacer and scoring the crankshaft seal surface.

mistakes.title: Drilling the rear seal without the spacer
mistakes.what: Drilling the rear seal without the JLR remover's depth-setting spacer.
mistakes.consequence: The bit runs on into the crankshaft seal surface or the cover and scores it, so the new seal leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Mount the JLR remover on its dowel and drill only through its guide at the set depth.

mistakes.title: Leaving drill swarf in the engine
mistakes.what: Leaving swarf from drilling the rear seal in the timing case and on the crank flange.
mistakes.consequence: Metal chips reach the oil pan and oil passages and score bearings on the rebuilt engine.
mistakes.prevent: Pack rag around the work area and vacuum out every chip before going further.

steps.title: Remove the lower timing cover
steps.action: Move the crankshaft position sensor aside, then remove the sixteen bolts and the lower timing cover, which doubles as the rear cover of the block.
steps.why: The cover is sealed with RTV silicone and spans the head gasket joint, so pry only at the provided points.

mistakes.title: Prying at the gasket joint
mistakes.what: Levering the lower timing cover off at any convenient spot rather than at the pry points.
mistakes.consequence: The cover or block face is gouged, and the cover spans the head gasket joint, so the gasket edge can be damaged too.
mistakes.prevent: Use only the provided pry points and lift the cover off square.

mistakes.title: Forgetting to move the crank sensor
mistakes.what: Pulling the cover without first moving the crankshaft position sensor aside.
mistakes.consequence: The sensor body or its mounting bracket snaps as the cover is pulled away.
mistakes.prevent: Move the sensor clear before removing the cover bolts.

steps.title: Remove the primary tensioner
steps.action: Remove the two bolts and the primary chain tensioner.

steps.title: Remove the primary chain guides
steps.action: Remove the primary chain tensioner guide and the fixed guide.

steps.title: Remove idler and primary chain
steps.action: Remove the idler sprocket bolt, lift off the idler sprocket and slip the primary chain off the crankshaft sprocket.

mistakes.title: Turning the crank with chains off
mistakes.what: Turning the crank with both chains off to make room or to check something.
mistakes.consequence: Pistons can rise into valves held open by the locked cams, and the timing reference is lost.
mistakes.prevent: Leave the crank locked until the chains are back on or the head is off.

steps.title: Remove the crankshaft pulley
steps.action: With the locking tool holding the crank, remove the four pulley bolts, then remove the tool and slide the pulley off its roll pin.
steps.why: The pulley carries the timing mark and the locking tool, so it stays on until the chains are off.
steps.mistake: Reusing the pulley bolts; the pulley procedure calls for four new bolts of the correct length.

mistakes.title: Reusing the crank pulley bolts
mistakes.what: Refitting the four old crank pulley bolts.
mistakes.consequence: Bolts already taken through an angle stage lose clamp, and the pulley that carries the timing reference can work loose.
mistakes.prevent: Fit four new 48 mm bolts; paint-mark the old ones and scrap them.

mistakes.title: Losing the pulley roll pin
mistakes.what: Pulling the crank pulley off and letting its roll pin fall out or get damaged.
mistakes.consequence: The pulley no longer locates correctly, so its timing mark and the locking tool reference are off.
mistakes.prevent: Check that the roll pin is still in the crank nose and undamaged before refitting.

steps.title: Remove the engine front cover
steps.action: Remove the twelve bolts and the front cover, then pull the front crank seal out with the JLR seal tool.

mistakes.title: Prying the front cover off
mistakes.what: Levering the engine front cover off on its sealing face.
mistakes.consequence: The face is marked and the cover leaks at the new RTV joint.
mistakes.prevent: Free the cover gently and clean, never gouge, its sealing face.

steps.title: Fit the CVVL locating pins
steps.action: Loosen the four specified CVVL bolts, remove two others, and screw the JLR locating pins into those two holes.
steps.why: The pins guide the CVVL unit straight up so its brake units and pumps are not side-loaded.

mistakes.title: Lifting the CVVL without locating pins
mistakes.what: Unbolting and lifting the CVVL unit without fitting the JLR locating pins.
mistakes.consequence: The unit tilts as it comes off and side-loads its brake units and pumps; it cannot be repaired, so damage means a new unit.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the locating pins in the specified holes and lift the unit straight up along them.

steps.title: Lift off the CVVL unit
steps.action: Remove the remaining bolts in the set sequence and lift the CVVL unit straight up, keeping it upright and holding it by its body, never by the solenoids.
steps.why: The unit is full of oil and is a non-serviceable assembly; turning it over or hanging it on the solenoids can ruin it.
steps.mistake: Turning the CVVL unit upside down to look at it, which lets air into the hydraulic circuits.

mistakes.title: Turning the CVVL unit upside down
mistakes.what: Flipping the CVVL unit over to look at its underside.
mistakes.consequence: Air gets into the oil-filled hydraulic chambers, and the sealed unit may then misfire or fail to switch valve lift.
mistakes.prevent: Keep the unit upright at all times and look at its underside with a mirror while it stays level.

mistakes.title: Carrying the CVVL by its solenoids
mistakes.what: Lifting or carrying the CVVL unit by its solenoids or connectors.
mistakes.consequence: The solenoids or their fragile connectors break, and the unit has no serviceable parts.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the unit by its body only and keep the connectors protected.

mistakes.title: Storing the CVVL unit uncovered
mistakes.what: Leaving the removed CVVL unit on the bench with its oil ports open to dust.
mistakes.consequence: The CVVL unit is already prone to failure from oil contamination, and dirt in its ports can jam the hydraulic chambers.
mistakes.prevent: Store the unit upright in a clean, covered box until it goes back on.

steps.title: Remove the camshaft setting tool
steps.action: Unbolt the camshaft setting tool from the camshafts.

steps.title: Lift off the camshaft carrier
steps.action: Remove the nineteen bolts and lift the camshaft carrier, with both camshafts inside it, off the head. Discard the gasket.
steps.why: The camshafts run in the carrier, not in the head.

mistakes.title: Prying the carrier off the head
mistakes.what: Levering the camshaft carrier off at its joint with the head.
mistakes.consequence: The sealing faces are gouged and the carrier gasket joint leaks oil.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the carrier straight up after all nineteen bolts are out, without wedging anything into the joint.

steps.title: Remove the intake camshaft
steps.action: Loosen the intake cam cap bolts one turn at a time in sequence, remove the five caps in order, and lift out the intake camshaft.
steps.why: Loosening gradually lets the valve and pump loads come off evenly so the hollow camshaft does not bend.
steps.mistake: Mixing up the caps; each is stamped I or E with a number and machined to its own bore.

mistakes.title: Piling the intake cam caps together
mistakes.what: Dropping the intake cam caps in a pile instead of keeping them in order.
mistakes.consequence: Each cap is machined with its own bore, so a cap in the wrong place pinches the camshaft and wears the bearing.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the caps out in order as they come off and read each I or E stamp and number.

mistakes.title: Releasing intake caps one at a time
mistakes.what: Unbolting one cam cap fully while the others still hold the camshaft down.
mistakes.consequence: Spring and pump loads bend or crack the camshaft, which is built up with pressed-on lobes.
mistakes.prevent: Loosen every cap bolt a turn at a time in sequence until the load is off.

steps.title: Remove the exhaust camshaft
steps.action: Loosen the exhaust cam cap bolts the same way, one turn at a time in sequence, then remove the five caps in order and lift out the exhaust camshaft.

mistakes.title: Releasing exhaust caps unevenly
mistakes.what: Loosening the exhaust cam caps out of sequence or one at a time.
mistakes.consequence: The exhaust camshaft is pushed up unevenly by the valve springs and can bend or crack.
mistakes.prevent: Loosen the exhaust caps a turn at a time in sequence, as for the intake.

steps.title: Remove head-mounted sensor and pipes
steps.action: Remove the cylinder head temperature sensor, the coolant pipe assembly and the coolant pipe at the head.

steps.title: Bag followers and lash adjusters
steps.action: Lift out the eight exhaust roller finger followers and eight hydraulic lash adjusters, keeping each in a labeled slot for its position.
steps.why: Parts that have worn in together must go back where they ran.

mistakes.title: Mixing follower and adjuster positions
mistakes.what: Dropping the roller followers and lash adjusters into one tray.
mistakes.consequence: Worn pairs end up on new partners, causing noise and faster wear on reused parts.
mistakes.prevent: Use a labeled rack and keep each follower and adjuster in its original position.

steps.title: Remove the small head bolts
steps.action: Remove the three small bolts and the single bolt at the timing end that tie the head to the block, before the main head bolts.

mistakes.title: Missing the small timing-end bolts
mistakes.what: Removing only the ten main head bolts before trying to lift the head.
mistakes.consequence: The three small bolts and the single bolt still hold the head, and levering against them can crack the head or block.
mistakes.prevent: Remove the small bolts at the timing end before the main head bolts.

steps.title: Loosen head bolts in sequence
steps.action: Using the JLR head bolt tool, loosen the ten main head bolts in the set sequence and discard them.
steps.why: Loosening in sequence keeps the head from distorting as clamp load comes off.
steps.mistake: Breaking the head bolts loose in random order.

mistakes.title: Loosening head bolts in random order
mistakes.what: Breaking the head bolts loose in whatever order is handy.
mistakes.consequence: Clamp load comes off unevenly and the aluminum head can warp, so it needs machining before it will seal.
mistakes.prevent: Loosen the ten bolts in the JLR sequence, a little at a time.

mistakes.title: Rounding head bolts with a generic bit
mistakes.what: Loosening the head bolts with a worn or wrong bit instead of the JLR head bolt tool.
mistakes.consequence: A bolt head rounds off and the bolt stays stuck in the block, needing extraction.
mistakes.prevent: Use the JLR-303-1653 tool, fully seated, for every head bolt.

steps.title: Lift off the cylinder head
steps.action: With a helper, lift the head straight off the dowels without levering on the gasket faces, then discard the head gasket and remove the two dowels.
steps.mistake: Prying between the head and block and gouging the aluminum sealing faces.

mistakes.title: Wedging tools between head and block
mistakes.what: Driving a pry bar or screwdriver into the head gasket joint to lift the head.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminum sealing faces are gouged, so the new gasket may not seal without machining.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the head straight up off its dowels with a helper, with nothing levered in the joint.

mistakes.title: Setting the head down on its face
mistakes.what: Laying the removed head deck-down on a dirty bench.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminum deck face is scratched and may need resurfacing before it will seal.
mistakes.prevent: Rest the head on blocks or its side on a clean surface.

steps.title: Remove the valves
steps.action: Compress each spring, remove the collets, spring and retainer, and keep every valve in a rack labeled by cylinder and position.

mistakes.title: Mixing up valves between guides
mistakes.what: Taking the valves out into one box instead of a numbered rack.
mistakes.consequence: Valves end up in different guides and seats, so lapped seat contact is lost and they may leak.
mistakes.prevent: Keep each valve in a rack labeled by cylinder and position.

steps.title: Discard the valve stem seals
steps.action: Pull and discard every valve stem seal, which also carries the spring seat.

mistakes.title: Gouging the guides pulling seals
mistakes.what: Prying out stem seals with a screwdriver or pliers that bite the guide top.
mistakes.consequence: The guides cannot be replaced on this head, so a damaged guide can mean a replacement head.
mistakes.prevent: Use a proper stem seal puller that grips only the seal.

steps.title: Remove the oil pan
steps.action: Remove the oil pan bolts, release the RTV seal at the pry points and lift off the cast aluminum pan.

mistakes.title: Prying the pan off anywhere
mistakes.what: Levering the oil pan off at random points along its joint.
mistakes.consequence: The cast pan or block face is gouged and the new RTV joint leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Release the seal only at the designed pry points.

mistakes.title: Not inspecting the pan contents
mistakes.what: Washing out the pan without looking at what was in it.
mistakes.consequence: You miss metal, sludge or sealant debris that explains a failure, so the cause is not fixed.
mistakes.prevent: Look through the sludge and debris in the pan and pickup before cleaning them.

steps.title: Remove the oil pump drive chain
steps.action: Hold the oil pump sprocket with the flange holding tool, remove and discard its bolt, and take off the drive chain and sprocket.

mistakes.title: Using the chain to hold the sprocket
mistakes.what: Loosening the oil pump sprocket bolt while relying on the chain or a screwdriver to stop it turning.
mistakes.consequence: The pump drive chain, its sprocket teeth or the pump shaft are strained and can be damaged.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the sprocket with the flange holding tool.

steps.title: Remove oil pump and pickup
steps.action: Unplug the pump solenoid, remove the pickup pipe bolt and four pump bolts, and lift off the variable-flow oil pump with its vacuum pump. Then separate the inlet pipe from the pump.

mistakes.title: Not checking the pickup screen
mistakes.what: Removing and cleaning the pickup without inspecting the screen.
mistakes.consequence: A screen clogged with sealant or sludge is a common cause of bearing starvation, and missing it hides the root cause.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the screen for sealant, sludge and metal before cleaning it.

steps.title: Remove the windage tray
steps.action: Remove the bolts and the cast aluminum structural windage tray from the bottom of the block.
steps.why: The tray stiffens the bottom end and covers the main caps and rod caps.

steps.title: Remove piston cooling jets
steps.action: Remove the single bolt on each of the four piston cooling jets and lift them out.
steps.why: The jets sit close to the bores and can be struck by a rod or the crank on the way out.
steps.mistake: Leaving the jets in and bending one while pushing out pistons or lifting the crank.

mistakes.title: Leaving the cooling jets in place
mistakes.what: Leaving the piston cooling jets in while the pistons and crank come out.
mistakes.consequence: A rod or crank throw bends a jet, which then misses its piston and lets the crown overheat after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Remove all four jets before pushing out any piston or lifting the crank.

steps.title: Mark rods and caps
steps.action: Confirm each rod and cap is marked to its cylinder and note the arrow on each piston crown toward the front.
steps.why: Rod caps are fracture-split and fit only their own rod in one orientation.

mistakes.title: Punching marks on fracture-split rods
mistakes.what: Marking rods and caps with a center punch or number stamps.
mistakes.consequence: Impact near the joint can damage a fracture-split rod, and a nick acts as a stress raiser.
mistakes.prevent: Check the factory pairing marks and add marks only with paint or a marker.

steps.title: Remove pistons and rods
steps.action: Remove each rod cap, protect the crank journal, and push the piston and rod out through the top of the bore, keeping the shells with their rod.

mistakes.title: Nicking the crank journal
mistakes.what: Pushing the rod out without protecting the journal from the rod bolts or rod end.
mistakes.consequence: A scratched journal needs regrinding, and JLR supplies graded rather than undersize shells.
mistakes.prevent: Fit protective sleeves or tape and guide the rod off the journal by hand.

mistakes.title: Resting the cap on its fracture face
mistakes.what: Laying rod caps on the bench on their split faces.
mistakes.consequence: The delicate fracture surface is damaged or soiled and the cap may no longer seat on its rod.
mistakes.prevent: Set caps down on their sides and refit each one loosely to its rod for storage.

mistakes.title: Losing the old shells' positions
mistakes.what: Throwing the used shells in a box together.
mistakes.consequence: You lose the wear pattern that tells you about oil supply, alignment or dirt in the old engine.
mistakes.prevent: Keep each pair of shells with its rod or cap and read the wear before scrapping them.

steps.title: Remove the main bearing caps
steps.action: Loosen the ten main cap bolts evenly and lift out the five numbered sintered-steel caps with their shells.

mistakes.title: Not confirming cap numbers
mistakes.what: Removing the main caps without checking that each is numbered and its arrow is readable.
mistakes.consequence: Caps get mixed or reversed on reassembly, shifting the bore and wiping the bearings.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the numbers and arrows before loosening any bolt, and mark any that are faint.

steps.title: Lift out the crankshaft
steps.action: Lift the crankshaft out of the block, then remove the two thrust washers at the center main and the upper shells.

mistakes.title: Knocking the crankshaft
mistakes.what: Leaning the crank against something hard or dropping it as it is lifted out.
mistakes.consequence: A journal is nicked or the crank is bent, and the crankshaft has to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the crank straight out with a helper and store it upright or supported along its length.

steps.title: Remove balancers and idler
steps.action: Remove the balancer idler gear, then withdraw both counter-rotating balancer shafts from their bores in the block.
steps.why: The balancers are gear-driven from a ring gear on the crankshaft, so the crank must come out first.

mistakes.title: Forcing balancer shafts out
mistakes.what: Pulling the balancer shafts out at an angle against their bearings.
mistakes.consequence: The needle rollers are dented (brinelled) or the outer races in the block are marked and must be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Withdraw each shaft straight along its bore after the idler gear is off.

steps.title: Separate pistons from rods
steps.action: Remove both circlips, push out the piston pin and separate each piston from its rod.

steps.title: Clean the gasket faces
steps.action: Remove the old gasket and RTV from the aluminum head, block and cover faces with a plastic scraper and solvent only.
steps.why: Metal scrapers and abrasive discs gouge aluminum and ruin the seal of the multi-layer steel (MLS) head gasket.
steps.mistake: Using an abrasive disc on the block deck.

mistakes.title: Using an abrasive disc on the deck
mistakes.what: Removing gasket residue from the block deck with an abrasive disc or pad.
mistakes.consequence: The disc takes metal off unevenly and sheds grit into the engine, so the deck is no longer flat and the gasket can leak.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the deck with a plastic scraper and solvent and plug every opening while you work.

mistakes.title: Using a steel scraper on aluminum
mistakes.what: Removing old gasket and RTV from the aluminum faces with a steel scraper or wire wheel.
mistakes.consequence: The faces are gouged and the MLS head gasket or RTV joints will not seal.
mistakes.prevent: Use a plastic scraper and solvent on all the sealing faces, as the head procedure requires.

mistakes.title: Letting cleaning grit into the galleries
mistakes.what: Letting abrasive dust and scraped residue fall into open oil and coolant passages.
mistakes.consequence: Grit circulates on first start and embeds in the new bearings, the most common cause of bearing failure.
mistakes.prevent: Plug the passages while cleaning the faces, then flush everything afterward.

mistakes.title: Leaving old RTV in grooves
mistakes.what: Leaving traces of old sealant in cover grooves and corners.
mistakes.consequence: New RTV does not bond, the joint leaks, and loose bits can reach the oil.
mistakes.prevent: Remove all old sealant and wipe the faces clean and dry just before applying new RTV.

steps.title: Flush every oil gallery
steps.action: Brush and flush the block, head and camshaft carrier oil galleries and blow them dry, looking for sludge in the high-pressure passages that feed the VCT and CVVL.
steps.why: JLR traced CVVL failures to oil sludge deposits in the high-pressure galleries; any left behind will lodge in the new parts.
steps.mistake: Fitting new timing parts or a new CVVL unit to galleries still holding old sludge.

mistakes.title: Fitting new parts to sludged galleries
mistakes.what: Fitting a new CVVL unit or new timing parts while old sludge is still in the high-pressure galleries.
mistakes.consequence: Loosened sludge travels into the new CVVL unit and phasers and brings the same failures back.
mistakes.prevent: Clean every high-pressure gallery until the solvent runs clear before any new part is fitted.

mistakes.title: Not flushing the oil cooler
mistakes.what: Cleaning the block and head but refitting the oil cooler without flushing it.
mistakes.consequence: Sludge and debris held in the cooler are pushed into the new bearings, phasers and CVVL unit.
mistakes.prevent: Flush the cooler thoroughly, or replace it if it cannot be cleaned or the engine failed with debris.

mistakes.title: Blowing out galleries without brushing
mistakes.what: Blowing the galleries out with air and nothing else.
mistakes.consequence: Packed sludge and debris stay in the passages and break loose later.
mistakes.prevent: Brush every gallery, flush with solvent and hot soapy water, then blow dry.

mistakes.title: Leaving water in the passages
mistakes.what: Leaving washed parts wet, or storing them before they are dried and oiled.
mistakes.consequence: Water left in passages and on bores causes corrosion and contaminates the first oil fill.
mistakes.prevent: Blow every passage dry straight after washing and oil the machined surfaces.

steps.title: Inspect VCT feed bores and dowels
steps.action: Clean the oil feed bores in the camshaft carrier that supply the phasers, and inspect each camshaft drive adapter and timing dowel.
steps.why: The phasers are moved by engine oil through these bores; a weak VCT seal or blocked feed causes the rattle and cam timing codes JLR documented.

mistakes.title: Ignoring a damaged VCT feed bore
mistakes.what: Passing over scored or blocked phaser oil feed bores in the camshaft carrier.
mistakes.consequence: The phaser gets less oil pressure, causing the rattle and cam timing codes the bulletin describes.
mistakes.prevent: Clean and inspect each feed bore; replace the part if a bore is scored.

mistakes.title: Missing a damaged timing dowel
mistakes.what: Overlooking a bent or burred camshaft timing dowel.
mistakes.consequence: The phaser cannot sit correctly on its dowel, so the cam is mistimed after reassembly.
mistakes.prevent: Check that each dowel is straight and clean and that the phaser slides onto it freely.

steps.title: Inspect the cylinder liners
steps.action: Check each thin-wall cast-iron liner for scoring, cracks and any movement at the deck.

mistakes.title: Missing a moved or cracked liner
mistakes.what: Giving the liners a quick look without checking for cracks or movement at the deck.
mistakes.consequence: A cracked or dropped liner leaks coolant or compression and needs a new or repaired block.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect each liner closely in good light and check that it is flush at the deck.

steps.title: Measure bores and pistons
steps.action: Measure each bore for taper and out-of-round, measure each piston skirt, and compare the two.
steps.why: JLR lists only one piston diameter grade, so a worn bore cannot be fixed with a factory oversize piston.

spec.note: nominal bore diameter; wear limits not published in sources found

mistakes.title: Measuring bores at one point
mistakes.what: Measuring each bore once instead of at several depths and in two directions.
mistakes.consequence: Taper and out-of-round are missed, and new rings will not seal in a worn bore.
mistakes.prevent: Measure top, middle and bottom in two directions at right angles and record the results.

steps.title: Check ring end gaps
steps.action: Square each new ring in its bore and check the end gap with feeler gauges.

mistakes.title: Measuring a cocked ring
mistakes.what: Pushing the ring into the bore by hand and measuring it while it is tilted.
mistakes.consequence: The gap reading is wrong, so the ring ends up too tight or too loose.
mistakes.prevent: Square each ring in the bore with a piston or ring squaring tool before measuring.

mistakes.title: Setting ring gaps too tight
mistakes.what: Skipping the end gap check, or accepting a gap at the tight end of the range on this turbocharged engine.
mistakes.consequence: The ring ends butt as they heat up, scuffing the bore and breaking the ring or piston land.
mistakes.prevent: Check every gap against the specification, remembering that boosted engines need more gap than non-turbo ones.

mistakes.title: Filing the ring gap wrongly
mistakes.what: Filing a gap from the inside out, crooked, or in big strokes.
mistakes.consequence: The ring face or coating chips, or the gap opens too far to recover.
mistakes.prevent: File from the outside in, in small amounts, keeping the ends square and checking often.

steps.title: Read the crankshaft codes
steps.action: Read the laser-etched letter strings or data-matrix code on the crankshaft for the main and rod journal grades.
steps.why: Bearing shells are chosen from these codes and the selection charts, not just from measuring.

mistakes.title: Misreading the crankshaft grade codes
mistakes.what: Misreading the letter strings or data-matrix code on the crank, or reading them from the wrong journal.
mistakes.consequence: The wrong shell grades are chosen and the running clearance is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Read the codes in good light, write them down journal by journal, and confirm with measurement.

mistakes.title: Polishing away the grade codes
mistakes.what: Cleaning the crank with an abrasive that removes the etched codes.
mistakes.consequence: Bearing selection then depends only on measurement, with more room for error.
mistakes.prevent: Record the codes before cleaning and clean the crank with solvent only.

steps.title: Measure the crank journals
steps.action: Measure every main and rod journal with a micrometer for size, taper and out-of-round, and check the induction-hardened surfaces for scoring.

mistakes.title: Measuring journals in one direction
mistakes.what: Measuring each journal once rather than in two directions and at both ends.
mistakes.consequence: Out-of-round or taper is missed and a worn crank is reused.
mistakes.prevent: Measure each journal in two directions at right angles and at both ends.

steps.title: Check bearing running clearance
steps.action: With the chosen shells fitted and the caps torqued, check main and rod clearances with Plastigage or a bore gauge and compare them with the selection chart.

mistakes.title: Using Plastigage on an oily journal
mistakes.what: Laying Plastigage on a journal or shell that still has oil on it.
mistakes.consequence: The strip does not crush properly and the clearance reads wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Wipe the journal and shell clean and dry before laying the strip.

mistakes.title: Turning the crank with Plastigage fitted
mistakes.what: Rotating the crank while the caps are torqued over the strips.
mistakes.consequence: The crushed strip smears into a wide band and gives a false, useless clearance reading.
mistakes.prevent: Leave the crank still until the cap is off and the strip has been read.

mistakes.title: Reading the narrowest part of the strip
mistakes.what: Comparing the crushed strip with the scale at its narrowest point only.
mistakes.consequence: Clearance looks larger than it is and taper goes unnoticed.
mistakes.prevent: Read the widest point and check both ends to see any taper.

mistakes.title: Measuring at the cap parting line
mistakes.what: Taking a bore gauge reading close to the cap parting line.
mistakes.consequence: The relief at the parting line makes the clearance look bigger than it is.
mistakes.prevent: Measure at 90 degrees to the parting line, with the caps torqued to assembly specification.

steps.title: Check head deck flatness
steps.action: Check the cylinder head face for distortion with a straightedge and feeler gauges across and diagonally.

mistakes.title: Checking the deck lengthwise only
mistakes.what: Laying the straightedge along the head only, not across and diagonally.
mistakes.consequence: Twist or cross-bow is missed and the gasket fails to seal.
mistakes.prevent: Check lengthwise, across and on both diagonals.

mistakes.title: Measuring over gasket residue
mistakes.what: Checking flatness before all the old gasket coating is removed.
mistakes.consequence: Residue lifts the straightedge and hides real distortion, or shows distortion that is not there.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the deck completely before measuring.

steps.title: Inspect valves and seats
steps.action: Inspect each valve face, stem and seat, and check the guides for wear by rocking each valve in its guide.

mistakes.title: Missing a bent valve
mistakes.what: Ignoring a low compression reading from before teardown when checking the valves.
mistakes.consequence: A bent valve goes back in and the cylinder leaks compression after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Check every valve for runout and seat contact, starting with any cylinder that tested low.

steps.title: Inspect camshafts and needle bearings
steps.action: Check the pressed-on cam lobes, the HP fuel pump lobe and the needle roller bearings for pitting or roughness.

mistakes.title: Ignoring HP fuel pump lobe wear
mistakes.what: Overlooking the HP fuel pump lobe on the exhaust camshaft.
mistakes.consequence: A worn lobe cannot drive the pump fully, giving low fuel pressure and early tappet or pump failure.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the pump lobe and the tappet face together and replace a worn camshaft.

mistakes.title: Passing rough cam needle bearings
mistakes.what: Reusing camshaft needle roller bearings without spinning them and checking for roughness.
mistakes.consequence: A failing bearing breaks up and sends needles and debris through the head.
mistakes.prevent: Spin and feel every bearing and replace any that is rough or pitted.

steps.title: Inspect followers and adjusters
steps.action: Check each exhaust roller follower for a free, smooth roller and each lash adjuster for wear.

mistakes.title: Reusing a flat-spotted follower roller
mistakes.what: Refitting an exhaust roller follower with a tight or flat-spotted roller.
mistakes.consequence: The roller skids on the lobe and wears both, giving valvetrain noise.
mistakes.prevent: Spin every roller and replace any that binds, feels rough or shows flats.

steps.title: Inspect balancer gears and bearings
steps.action: Check the balancer needle bearings, the outer races in the block, the helical gear teeth and the anti-backlash scissor gears.

mistakes.title: Reusing a weak scissor gear
mistakes.what: Reusing the anti-backlash scissor gears on the balancer drive without checking their spring action.
mistakes.consequence: Weak scissor gears let the gears rattle at idle.
mistakes.prevent: Check that each scissor gear springs back freely and replace it if weak or chipped.

mistakes.title: Reusing pitted balancer bearings
mistakes.what: Reusing balancer needle bearings or races that show pitting.
mistakes.consequence: A failing balancer bearing makes noise and can shed debris into the oil.
mistakes.prevent: Replace bearings and races that show pitting or roughness.

steps.title: Inspect the turbocharger
steps.action: Check the turbo shaft for radial and axial play, wheel contact and coked oil in the center housing, and confirm the oil feed and return pipes are clear.
steps.why: A turbo that failed from oil starvation or contamination will fail again on a fresh engine.

mistakes.title: Refitting a turbo with shaft play
mistakes.what: Refitting a turbo with excessive play or wheel rub to the fresh engine.
mistakes.consequence: The turbo fails soon, and a failing compressor wheel can shed pieces into the intake.
mistakes.prevent: Replace the turbo if it shows wheel contact or play beyond the maker's limits.

mistakes.title: Replacing a turbo without finding the cause
mistakes.what: Replacing a failed turbo without finding out why it failed.
mistakes.consequence: Most turbo failures are oil-related, so the new one fails the same way.
mistakes.prevent: Check oil supply, oil condition, the feed and drain lines and the intake for the cause before fitting a new turbo.

mistakes.title: Not cleaning the charge-air path
mistakes.what: Reusing the charge-air pipes and cooler uncleaned after a turbo failure.
mistakes.consequence: Fragments and oil left in the cooler are drawn into the new turbo and engine.
mistakes.prevent: Clean or replace the charge-air cooler and pipes after any turbo wheel failure.

steps.title: Assess the CVVL unit
steps.action: Decide whether the CVVL unit is reused or replaced; it is a sealed assembly, and a failed solenoid, sludge or misfire history means a new unit.
steps.why: JLR does not sell CVVL solenoids or internals; the only repair is a complete unit.

mistakes.title: Reusing a sludged CVVL unit
mistakes.what: Passing a CVVL unit with sludge or a history of degraded oil for reuse.
mistakes.consequence: Sludge inside the unit causes misfires and limp running after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Replace the CVVL unit when sludge or misfire history is present.

mistakes.title: Opening the CVVL to repair it
mistakes.what: Dismantling the CVVL unit to clean it or replace a solenoid.
mistakes.consequence: The unit is a sealed, non-serviceable assembly, and opening it ruins it.
mistakes.prevent: Treat the unit as a single part: reuse it complete or replace it complete.

steps.title: Decide on valve work
steps.action: Have the seats and valves refaced only as needed, then lap each valve until a continuous contact band shows on both valve and seat.

mistakes.title: Leaving lapping paste in the head
mistakes.what: Leaving lapping compound on stems, guides or in the ports.
mistakes.consequence: The abrasive wears the guides and new stem seals and reaches the oil.
mistakes.prevent: Clean every valve, seat and port thoroughly after lapping.

steps.title: Replace the head if guides are worn
steps.action: If guide wear is out of limits, plan on a replacement head.
steps.why: JLR lists the valve guides as non-serviceable.

mistakes.title: Building on worn valve guides
mistakes.what: Rebuilding a head whose guides are beyond limits anyway.
mistakes.consequence: Valves seat poorly and oil is drawn past the stem seals, and the guides cannot be replaced to factory standard.
mistakes.prevent: Measure the guides and plan a replacement head if they are out of limits.

steps.title: Decide the bore strategy
steps.action: Within limits, hone lightly and fit new rings; with liner scoring or wear beyond limits, replace the block or send it to a specialist for sleeving.
steps.why: JLR offers one piston size and interference-fit liners, so there is no factory oversize route.
